about: What each U.S. state legislature needs to ratify a proposed amendment to the U.S. Constitution that Congress has sent to the state legislatures under Article V, researched from the state constitutions, the chambers' rules, state statutes, state attorney general opinions, court decisions, and the NCSL and Congressional Research Service surveys, as of 2026-10-01. This is the binding Team 2's A79 ratification roll call reads: one row per state (50), one entry per chamber (Nebraska has one), giving the vote a chamber needs (threshold), the quorum, how fractions round, and any extra condition. Read threshold.basis first: 'elected' means a fraction of all members elected or entitled (absent members count against), 'present' means a fraction of members present and voting with a quorum. Every threshold carries a ruleKind that says how firmly it is sourced; the kinds that say 'assumed', 'default' or 'unsourced' are inferences from a general rule, not a rule about ratification, and each says so in its notes. Federal law governs the act: the Supreme Court has held that ratifying is a federal function that a state constitution cannot limit (Hawke v. Smith, 1920; Leser v. Garnett, 1922, both discussed in Idaho Attorney General Opinion 86-9), so some on-the-books state limits (Kansas's two-thirds clause, the intervening-election clauses of Florida, Illinois and Tennessee) may not bind. They are recorded as conditions or onTheBooks so the game can show them without applying them blindly.

threshold.basis: 'elected' = fraction of all members elected or entitled to the chamber (the rule's denominator; some rules exclude vacancies, see rounding). 'present' = fraction of members present for the vote, a quorum being present.
threshold.strictlyGreater: true: yes votes must be MORE than fraction x basis (a majority). false: yes votes must be AT LEAST fraction x basis, rounded up to a whole member (a supermajority).
threshold.presentMeans: only with basis 'present'. 'present-and-voting' = members who vote count; 'members-present' = everyone in attendance counts, so an abstention counts against.
threshold.alsoRequires: extra floor. minYesFractionOfElected: yes votes must also be at least that fraction of members elected (Kentucky, Virginia: two-fifths).
threshold.minimumVotes: An explicit fixed affirmative-vote floor stated by the ratification instrument. It stays required even when the fractional denominator is smaller.

schema.quorum: The number of members that must be present for the chamber to act: fraction of members elected or entitled; strictlyGreater true means more than that fraction. Optional citationIndex identifies the quorum citation separately from the affirmative-vote source.
schema.rounding: Plain-words statement of how to count, and any count the rule itself states.

ruleKind.ratification-specific: A rule, statute or constitutional clause names ratifying a federal amendment and states the vote.
ruleKind.ratification-specific-unenforced: A clause names ratification and states a vote, but an attorney general or court says it cannot bind (Kansas); the applied threshold is the fallback and onTheBooks holds the stated one.
ruleKind.resolution-rule: A rule or clause states the vote for the kind of resolution used to ratify, but does not name federal ratification.
ruleKind.bill-rule-by-reference: A rule or clause says ratifying resolutions are treated as bills (or joint resolutions are held to the bill vote), so the bill vote applies.
ruleKind.bill-rule-assumed: INFERRED: only the constitutional vote for a bill was found; applied to a ratifying resolution without a rule saying so.
ruleKind.default: No ratification or resolution vote found; the chamber's ordinary-question rule or practice is applied, with its citation.
ruleKind.default-unsourced: No ordinary-question rule located either; the general parliamentary default (majority of those voting, quorum present) is applied. Needs a human check.

schema.onTheBooks: A stated rule that is not applied (see ruleKind ratification-specific-unenforced).
schema.conditions: Extra conditions apart from the vote: intervening-election clauses, an advisory-election statute, and New Hampshire's thin-attendance two-thirds rule.
schema.sameResolutionBothChambers: true for every state: the legislature acts by one resolution, in the same text, adopted by each chamber separately; no state lets one chamber ratify alone. Governor involvement is recorded in governorRole where a rule or constitution says something.
schema.citations: text is the rule's own words with its location; url is where it was read; accessed is the date read. Where the official text could not be fetched, the 50 Constitutions compilation (University of Wisconsin Law School State Democracy Research Initiative) is cited and says so.
schema.ratificationBridge: Only for bill-rule-by-reference or resolution-rule: kind sourced-form-and-vote-rule plus formCitationIndex, procedureCitationIndex, thresholdCitationIndex and quorumCitationIndex into this chamber's citations. Each role must cite the ratification instrument/procedure, vote or quorum source; a general bill or parliamentary inference never supplies this bridge.

article.text: U.S. Constitution, Article V: "when ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof, as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress;"

surveyNote.text: NCSL's 1995 survey, quoted by CRS Report 97-922, counted seven states that require a supermajority in one or more chambers, by rule, statute or constitution: Alabama, Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois and Kansas. Checked against the current texts: Alabama (House only), Colorado (House only), Illinois and Kansas (on the books, unenforced) still have one; Delaware dropped its two-thirds statute (now a majority); no supermajority was found for Georgia or Idaho. Other differences from a plain majority (a two-thirds quorum in Indiana, Oregon, Tennessee and Texas; a two-fifths floor in Kentucky and Virginia; New Hampshire's thin-attendance rule; the intervening-election clauses) are recorded in each row.

citations.text: (1) Each bill passed by the legislature, except bills proposing amendments to the Montana constitution, bills ratifying proposed amendments to the United States constitution, resolutions, and initiative and referendum measures, shall be submitted to the governor for his signature. If he does not sign or veto the bill within 10 days after its delivery to him, it shall become law. The governor shall return a vetoed bill to the legislature with a statement of his reasons therefor. (2) The governor may return any bill to the legislature with his recommendation for amendment. If the legislature passes the bill in accordance with the governor's recommendation, it shall again return the bill to the governor for his reconsideration. The governor shall not return a bill for amendment a second time. (3) If after receipt of a veto message, two-thirds of the members of each house present approve the bill, it shall become law. (4) (a) If the legislature is not in session when the governor vetoes a bill approved by two-thirds of the members present, he shall return the bill with his reasons therefor to the secretary of state. The secretary of state shall poll the members of the legislature by mail and shall send each member a copy of the governor's veto message. If two-thirds or more of the members of each house vote to override the veto, the bill shall become law. (b) The legislature may reconvene as provided by law to reconsider any bill vetoed by the governor when the legislature is not in session. (5) The governor may veto items in appropriation bills, and in such instances the procedure shall be the same as upon veto of an entire bill.

No bill shall become law except by a vote of the majority of all members present and voting. (2) Every vote of each member of the legislature on each substantive question in the legislature, in any committee, or in committee of the whole shall be recorded and made public. On final passage, the vote shall be taken by ayes and noes and the names entered on the journal.
